title: What Happens When You Open a Website?

sources.title: RFC 1034: Domain Names — Concepts and Facilities
sources.notes: Checked resolver, hierarchy and cache behavior; narrative uses a deliberately simplified uncached lookup.

sources.title: RFC 9112: HTTP/1.1
sources.notes: Checked request/response framing and connection management; this episode uses a teaching example of HTTP/1.1 over TCP.

sources.title: RFC 9293: Transmission Control Protocol
sources.notes: Checked ports, sequence numbers and connection establishment.

sources.title: RFC 9114: HTTP/3
sources.notes: Checked HTTP/3 maps HTTP semantics onto QUIC rather than TCP.

sections.title: One click, many conversations
sections.narration: A page appears after one click. But the server could be across an ocean, and your computer started with only a name. How does that tiny action become a complete journey? Follow this request.
sections.takeaway: Opening a website is a sequence of coordinated network tasks.

sections.title: Choose a clear teaching model
sections.narration: We'll slow down a first visit using HTTP version one point one over TCP. Browsers often reuse earlier work. Leaving those shortcuts aside lets us see the separate decisions hidden inside an ordinary page load.
sections.takeaway: This example explains one path, not every modern browser connection.

sections.title: From LAN to WAN
sections.narration: Our request first crosses a local network, then enters a chain of other networks. The Internet is this interconnection. No single cable stretches from every browser to every website; routers join the pieces together.
sections.takeaway: The Internet connects many separate networks.

sections.title: Layers divide the work
sections.narration: Notice how many different jobs are already appearing. Layers separate those jobs. OSI describes seven; this TCP/IP picture groups them into four. They're different ways to organize responsibilities, rather than physical floors inside the computer.
sections.takeaway: OSI and TCP/IP group related communication responsibilities differently.

sections.title: Ask for an address
sections.narration: The browser has a name, but packets need an address. DNS supplies that missing link. We ask a resolver to find the address associated with the name, turning something readable into something the network can use.
sections.takeaway: DNS helps translate a useful name into addressing information.

sections.title: Follow the DNS hierarchy
sections.narration: Without a cached answer, the resolver follows referrals: root, top-level domain, then the authoritative server. Each reply narrows the search. No single directory needs to store the complete answer for every name on the Internet.
sections.takeaway: An uncached DNS lookup may follow several referrals.

sections.title: Reuse a cached answer
sections.narration: Now repeat the lookup. The saved answer avoids the earlier search, so the path gets shorter. A cache makes previous work useful again, but only within its allowed lifetime. Old directions can eventually become wrong.
sections.takeaway: A cached DNS answer can shorten the next visit.

sections.title: Choose the receiving process
sections.narration: Reaching the right computer is only part of delivery. Which application should receive the data? Ports distinguish endpoints there. Our client uses 49152; the server uses 80. The address and port answer different questions.
sections.takeaway: An IP address alone does not select the receiving application.

sections.title: Establish a TCP connection
sections.narration: Before the request, three TCP messages cross the link: SYN, SYN with ACK, then ACK. Each side establishes connection state. The connection is shared agreement between endpoints; the network hasn't reserved a private physical path.
sections.takeaway: The TCP handshake establishes connection state at both ends.

sections.title: Build the HTTP request
sections.narration: Now the browser can ask for the resource. GET supplies the HTTP meaning; TCP carries the bytes. Notice the separation: transporting a request successfully doesn't tell us whether the requested page exists.
sections.takeaway: HTTP describes what the application wants.

sections.title: Wrap the application bytes
sections.narration: Watch the blue message stay inside as new information appears around it. This is encapsulation: each layer adds what its own job needs. A larger message can also be divided across several transport segments.
sections.takeaway: Encapsulation packages one layer's data for the next layer.

sections.title: Transport adds its information
sections.narration: TCP adds ports and sequence information, identifying the conversation and locating bytes within it. The application data remains inside. A boundary between application writes doesn't necessarily become a boundary between segments on the wire.
sections.takeaway: TCP organizes a byte stream into segments for transmission.

sections.title: Address the IP packet
sections.narration: Next come the IP source and destination. Routers can use the destination to choose where the packet goes next. The server remains our goal here, though mechanisms such as address translation can alter addresses.
sections.takeaway: IP addressing supports delivery across interconnected networks.

sections.title: Prepare the local frame
sections.narration: The outer frame answers a more immediate question: who receives this on the local link? For a distant server, that may be the gateway. The next local destination and the final IP destination serve different purposes.
sections.takeaway: A link-layer frame serves one local link.

sections.title: Turn bits into signals
sections.narration: All those headers and bytes must now become a physical signal. Copper, fiber, and radio do this differently. The travelling marks represent changing signals, not tiny printed digits being pushed through a cable.
sections.takeaway: Physical transmission carries encoded information over a medium.

sections.title: The switch forwards a frame
sections.narration: At the switch, the frame takes a local turn based on MAC forwarding information. Watch the selected output. This decision moves data within the local network; it doesn't calculate the entire route to the website.
sections.takeaway: A switch forwards within its link-layer domain.

sections.title: The router chooses a next hop
sections.narration: The router removes the incoming frame and examines the IP destination. It chooses a next hop without needing to interpret GET. A useful network can move many kinds of application data using the same forwarding machinery.
sections.takeaway: Routers connect networks by forwarding IP packets.

sections.title: New frame, continuing packet
sections.narration: Here is the detail to watch: the local frame changes, while our request continues toward the server. Each routed hop gets its own link information. One journey is being carried through several separate local deliveries.
sections.takeaway: Link-layer envelopes are replaced as a packet crosses routers.

sections.title: Shared links can queue or lose
sections.narration: A shared outgoing link creates a bottleneck. Packets arrive faster than it can send them, so a queue grows. When the buffer fills, packets may be dropped. Connectivity alone doesn't promise immediate or successful delivery.
sections.takeaway: Packets share limited resources along the path.

sections.title: Unwrap at the server
sections.narration: At the server, the wrapping comes off in stages: link, IP, TCP, then HTTP. Each layer handles its own information and passes the useful contents upward. The application finally receives the request we started with.
sections.takeaway: Decapsulation lets each receiving layer perform its own job.

sections.title: Send an HTTP response
sections.narration: The server returns status information and content. Those bytes need the same layered delivery in reverse. But reverse doesn't require an identical route: the response can cross a different sequence of networks on its way back.
bullets: The response takes a return path
sections.takeaway: The server sends a new application message back.

sections.title: A page can trigger more requests
sections.narration: That response may contain instructions to fetch images, styles, and other resources. So one apparent page load becomes several conversations, sometimes involving other servers or caches. The first arrival starts another round of work.
sections.takeaway: One visible page can require many resource transfers.
sections.short_title: Fetch the rest of the page

sections.title: Add the modern distinctions
sections.narration: Our example used HTTP over TCP. HTTPS adds TLS protection, while HTTP version three uses QUIC over UDP. Different protocols can fill these roles, but the underlying questions about names, endpoints, and delivery still remain.
sections.takeaway: The web uses several protocol combinations, not only HTTP over TCP.

sections.title: Retell the whole journey
sections.narration: Return to the opening click. A name became an address, bytes gained headers, and routers connected local steps into one journey. The remarkable part is how many small agreements cooperate to produce something that feels immediate.
sections.takeaway: A page load succeeds because multiple protocols perform distinct jobs.
